record.paper_title: QM2017: Status and Key open Questions in Ultra-Relativistic Heavy-Ion Physics
record.original_question: Does the initial temperature inferred from excess direct photons in heavy-ion collisions increase from RHIC to LHC energies, and can higher-precision photon measurements plus calculations with medium-modified rates and state-of-the-art space-time evolution establish that trend?

evidence.quote: The inverse slopes of the direct photon excess (≈200 MeV at RHIC and ≈300 MeV at LHC) can be related to a temperature only in a model dependent way (because of space-time averaging and flow blue shift), but indicate initial temperatures of order T0 ≈300 - 500 MeV, far above Tc.

A number of key issues remain to be addressed for direct photons: on the experimental side primarily reducing errors (stat+syst) to confirm that T0 indeed increases with energy between RHIC and LHC, as the current evidence is only marginally significant; on the theory side more detailed calculations including e.g. medium effects on rates and state-of-the-art space-time evolution.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, the transverse-momentum spectrum of "direct photons" (the inclusive photon yield with hadron-decay contributions subtracted) exhibits, in the soft region (roughly 1 ≲ p_T ≲ 4 GeV), an exponential excess above prompt-photon (next-to-leading-order pQCD) baselines. This excess is commonly characterized by an inverse logarithmic slope T_eff defined via fitting dN/(p_T dp_T) ∝ exp(−p_T / T_eff). Through a hydrodynamic / fireball model of the collision evolution, T_eff is related (with corrections from space-time averaging over the fireball history and from blue-shifting due to collective transverse flow) to an inferred initial fireball temperature T_0 at the thermalization time τ_0.

Available measurements give T_eff ≈ 200 MeV at top RHIC energy (Au+Au at √s_NN = 200 GeV) and T_eff ≈ 300 MeV at LHC energies (Pb+Pb at √s_NN = 2.76 TeV), with corresponding model-extracted initial temperatures in the range T_0 ≈ 300–500 MeV, well above the QCD pseudo-critical temperature T_c ≈ 155 MeV.

Question. Establish, using improved direct-photon measurements (reduced statistical and systematic uncertainties) together with theoretical thermal-photon-rate calculations that incorporate medium modifications and a state-of-the-art (3+1)-dimensional viscous relativistic hydrodynamic space-time evolution coupled to a realistic initial-state model, whether the inferred initial temperature T_0(√s_NN) is a strictly increasing function of collision energy between √s_NN = 200 GeV and √s_NN = 2.76 TeV (and at higher LHC energies). Quantify the magnitude of the increase ΔT_0 with statistical significance ≥ 3σ.
artifact.status_search_result: As of 2026, while direct-photon measurements at RHIC and LHC continue to indicate higher inferred initial temperatures at LHC than at RHIC (with hydrodynamic extractions reaching ≳500 MeV), the experimental and theoretical uncertainties remain large and the energy dependence of T_0 has not been established with the high precision called for. The question therefore appears still open.

status_evidence.title: Properties of thermal photons at RHIC and LHC
status_evidence.snippet: Compilation of effective temperatures as a function of center-of-mass energy from RHIC and LHC direct-photon measurements.
status_evidence.claim: T_eff values at RHIC and LHC are compiled but uncertainties limit firm conclusions on the trend.

status_evidence.title: Temperature of the QGP: a brief overview
status_evidence.snippet: Hydrodynamic analyses extract initial temperatures of order 500 MeV from direct-photon data, with substantial model dependence.
status_evidence.claim: Model-dependent extractions of T_0 from direct photons remain the state of the art.

status_evidence.title: Mean free path of photons in relativistic heavy ion collisions
status_evidence.snippet: Recent (2025) work continues to refine theoretical thermal-photon rates and transport in QGP.
status_evidence.claim: Theoretical refinements of photon emission rates and transport are still ongoing.
